rows.stem: In a region, the electric potential varies as \(V = 10 - 50x\), where V is in volts and \(x\) in meters. The electric field in the region is :
rows.solution:
The field is the negative gradient of the potential:

\(E_x = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}\)

With \(V = 10 - 50x\):

\(\dfrac{dV}{dx} = -50 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_x = -(-50) = +50\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\)

A positive \(E_x\) means the field points along \(+x\), so the field is **50 N/C along \(+x\)** — option (C).

Two checks are worth carrying. The **magnitude** is the coefficient of \(x\) alone; the constant 10 V contributes nothing, since a uniform offset in potential produces no field. And the **direction** follows from the minus sign in the definition: the potential *decreases* as \(x\) increases here, and the field always points from high potential to low, hence along \(+x\).

Options (A) and (B) take the constant term as the field, which is the commonest slip.

rows.stem: A conducting wire connects two charged metallic spheres A and B of radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) respectively. The distance between the spheres is very large compared to their radii. The ratio of electric fields, \((E_A/E_B)\) at the surfaces of spheres A and B will be
rows.solution:
Joining the spheres with a wire forces them to a **common potential** — that is the only thing the connection does, and everything follows from it.

For an isolated sphere carrying charge \(Q\),

\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r} \qquad\text{and}\qquad E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^{2}}\)

Dividing one by the other:

\(E = \dfrac{V}{r}\)

Since the wire makes \(V\) the same for both spheres,

\(\dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = \dfrac{V/r_1}{V/r_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\)

The answer is (B).

The result is worth remembering in the form it takes: on connected conductors the field at the surface — and likewise the surface charge density — goes as \(1/r\), so the **smaller** sphere ends up with the **stronger** field. This is why charge concentrates at points and sharp edges on a conductor, and it is the principle behind the lightning rod.

The condition that the separation is large compared with the radii is what allows each sphere to be treated as isolated and uniformly charged; placed close together they would polarise each other and the simple formulae would fail.

rows.subtopic: Ampere's Circuital Law and the Solenoid
rows.stem: A long straight wire of circular cross-section (radius a) carries a steady current I. The current is uniformly distributed across this cross-section. The magnitude of the magnetic field produced at a point at a distance (a/2) from the axis of the wire will be
rows.solution:
The point lies **inside** the conductor, at \(r = a/2 < a\), so Ampère's law must be applied to the current actually enclosed — not the whole current \(I\).

Take a circular Amperian loop of radius \(r\) coaxial with the wire. Since the current is uniformly distributed over the cross-section, the enclosed fraction is the area ratio:

\(I_{\text{enc}} = I\,\dfrac{\pi r^{2}}{\pi a^{2}} = I\,\dfrac{r^{2}}{a^{2}}\)

Ampère's law gives

\(B \times 2\pi r = \mu_0 I\,\dfrac{r^{2}}{a^{2}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^{2}}\)

So inside the wire the field grows **linearly** with distance from the axis. At \(r = a/2\):

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a^{2}} \times \dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\)

The answer is (C).

Option (B) is the field at the **surface** \((r = a)\), which is exactly twice this — the linear growth means halving the radius halves the field. Option (A) would be correct only on the axis itself, where no current is enclosed at all.

rows.stem: The shape of the interference fringes in Young's double-slit experiment, when the distance between the slit and the screen is very large as compared to the slit-separation, is nearly
rows.solution:
The locus of points with a constant path difference from two sources is a **hyperbola**, so the fringes are strictly hyperbolic in shape.

But the question asks what they are *nearly*, in the limit \(D \gg d\). In that regime the screen intercepts only the small central portion of each hyperbola, close to its vertex, where the curvature is negligible over the width of the pattern. The fringes therefore appear as **straight** bands, parallel to the slits.

The answer is (A).

The approximation is the same one that underlies the whole of the standard treatment: it is what licenses writing the path difference as \(xd/D\) and hence the fringe width as \(\lambda D/d\). The hyperbolic curvature only becomes visible if the screen is brought close to the slits, or if a very wide field of view is examined.

rows.stem: An electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into a dielectric medium with relative electrical permittivity (3/2) and relative magnetic permeability (8/3). Then, its

options.label: A
options.text: wavelength is doubled and frequency remains unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: wavelength is doubled and frequency is halved.

options.label: C
options.text: wavelength is halved and frequency remains unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: wavelength and frequency both will remain unchanged.

rows.solution:
The refractive index of a medium is fixed by both of its electromagnetic constants:

\(n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}\)

Substituting the given values:

\(n = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{8}{3}} = \sqrt{4} = 2\)

**Frequency.** Frequency is a property of the **source** and cannot change at a boundary — if it did, wave crests would have to pile up at or vanish from the interface. So the frequency **remains unchanged**.

**Wavelength.** The speed falls to \(v = c/n = c/2\), and since \(v = \nu\lambda\) with \(\nu\) fixed, the wavelength must fall in step:

\(\lambda_{\text{medium}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{n} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\)

So the wavelength is **halved** and the frequency is unchanged — option (C).

The question is built so that neither constant alone gives the answer: \(\varepsilon_r = 3/2\) and \(\mu_r = 8/3\) are individually awkward, and it is only their **product** that comes out as the clean perfect square 4. A magnetic medium like this is unusual — for most optical materials \(\mu_r \approx 1\) and \(n \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\) — which is exactly why the question specifies both.

rows.stem: In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the resistor, capacitor and inductor is 10 V each. If the capacitor is short circuited, the voltage across the inductor will be
rows.solution:
The initial condition tells us more than it appears to. With \(V_R = V_L = V_C = 10\) V, the inductive and capacitive voltages are equal, so \(X_L = X_C\): the circuit is **at resonance**. The applied voltage is then

\(V = \sqrt{V_R^{2} + (V_L - V_C)^{2}} = V_R = 10\ \text{V}\)

And since the same current flows through all three, \(V_L = V_R\) means

\(X_L = R\)

**After the capacitor is short-circuited** the circuit is a series LR across the same 10 V supply:

\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + R^{2}} = R\sqrt{2}\)

\(I' = \dfrac{V}{Z} = \dfrac{10}{R\sqrt{2}}\)

\(V_L' = I'X_L = \dfrac{10}{R\sqrt{2}} \times R = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\sqrt{2}\ \text{V}\)

The answer is (B), about \(7{\cdot}07\) V.

The voltage across the inductor **falls** — from 10 V to \(5\sqrt{2}\) V — even though removing the capacitor removes an obstacle. The reason is that at resonance the inductor and capacitor cancel each other exactly, leaving only \(R\) to limit the current; shorting the capacitor destroys that cancellation, the impedance rises from \(R\) to \(R\sqrt{2}\), and the smaller current produces a smaller voltage across \(X_L\).

rows.stem: Electromagnetic waves used in a diagnostic tool in medicine have a wavelength range
rows.solution:
The diagnostic tool in question is **X-ray radiography**, and X-rays span roughly \(1\ \mathrm{nm}\) down to \(10^{-3}\ \mathrm{nm}\) — option (A).

X-rays are suited to it because of where their photon energy sits: high enough to pass through soft tissue without being absorbed, but low enough that the calcium in bone absorbs them strongly. Bone therefore casts a shadow on the detector, and a fracture appears as a discontinuity in that shadow.

The other ranges name different regions and different uses: 400 nm to 1 nm is the **ultraviolet**, 1 mm to 700 nm the **infrared**, and 0·1 m to 1 mm the **microwave** band. None of them penetrates the body usefully — UV is absorbed within the outermost layers of skin, and infrared and microwaves are absorbed by water.

rows.stem: The 'distance of closest approach' of an alpha-particle is 'd' when it moves with a velocity \(\nu\) head-on towards the target nucleus. If the velocity of alpha particle is halved, the new 'distance of closest approach' will be -
rows.solution:
At the distance of closest approach the particle has stopped, so all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{d} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4Ze^{2}}{mv^{2}}\)

Everything on the right except \(v\) is fixed by the projectile and the target, so

\(d \propto \dfrac{1}{v^{2}}\)

Halving the velocity therefore **quadruples** the distance:

\(d' = \dfrac{d}{(1/2)^{2}} = 4d\)

The answer is (D).

The square is the point of the question. The dependence runs through the kinetic energy, which itself goes as \(v^{2}\), so the effect of changing the speed is doubled. Halving \(v\) leaves the alpha particle with only a quarter of its energy, and it therefore runs out of energy four times further from the nucleus.

Option (B), \(2d\), is what a linear dependence on \(v\) would give.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A concave lens of focal length 10 cm is cut into two identical plano-concave lenses. The focal length of each lens will be
rows.solution:
To be cut into two **plano-concave** lenses, the original equiconcave lens must be sliced **perpendicular to the principal axis** — each half keeps one curved face and acquires one plane face.

For the original equiconcave lens with both radii of magnitude \(R\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(-\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = -(\mu - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

Each half has one plane surface \((R \to \infty)\) and one concave surface of radius \(R\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = (\mu - 1)\left(-\dfrac{1}{R} - 0\right) = -(\mu - 1)\dfrac{1}{R}\)

Comparing, \(\dfrac{1}{f'} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{f}\), so

\(f' = 2f = 2 \times 10 = 20\ \text{cm}\)

The answer is (A).

Each half has lost one of its two refracting surfaces, so it has half the power and twice the focal length. The contrast with the other cut is worth holding: slicing **along** the principal axis would leave both curved surfaces intact on each half, and the focal length would be **unchanged** at 10 cm — only the aperture, and hence the image brightness, would halve.

rows.stem:
Four independent waves are expressed as
(i) \(y_1 = A_1 \sin \omega t\)
(ii) \(y_2 = A_2 \sin 2 \omega t\)
(iii) \(y_3 = A_3 \cos \omega t\)
(iv) \(y_4 = A_4 \sin (\omega t + \pi/3)\)
The interference between two of these waves is possible in
rows.solution:
Interference requires the two waves to have the **same frequency** and a **constant phase difference**. Comparing the four:

- \(y_1 = A_1\sin\omega t\) — frequency \(\omega\)
- \(y_2 = A_2\sin 2\omega t\) — frequency \(2\omega\)
- \(y_3 = A_3\cos\omega t = A_3\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) — frequency \(\omega\)
- \(y_4 = A_4\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\) — frequency \(\omega\)

Three of them — **(i), (iii) and (iv)** — share the frequency \(\omega\), and each pair drawn from them has a phase difference that is a fixed number \(\left(\pi/2,\ \pi/3,\ \pi/6\right)\). Any two of the three can interfere.

Only \(y_2\) is excluded, its frequency being \(2\omega\).

The answer is (C).

The step that decides it is recognising \(\cos\omega t\) as \(\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)\): written as a cosine it looks like a different kind of function, but it is the same frequency with a quarter-cycle head start. Equal **amplitudes** are not required — unequal amplitudes still interfere, merely with imperfect contrast, since \(I_{\min} = \left(\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}\right)^{2}\) vanishes only when the two are equal.

rows.stem: Two heaters rated as \((P_1, V)\) and \((P_2, V)\) are connected in series across a dc source of \(\frac{V}{2}\) volt. The power consumed by the combination will be -
rows.solution:
A rating \((P, V)\) fixes each heater's **resistance**, which is the quantity that survives the change of supply:

\(R_1 = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P_1}, \qquad R_2 = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P_2}\)

**In series** the resistances add:

\(R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 = V^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{P_1} + \dfrac{1}{P_2}\right) = \dfrac{V^{2}(P_1 + P_2)}{P_1P_2}\)

**Across a supply of \(V/2\):**

\(P = \dfrac{(V/2)^{2}}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{V^{2}/4}{\dfrac{V^{2}(P_1+P_2)}{P_1P_2}} = \dfrac{P_1P_2}{4(P_1 + P_2)}\)

The answer is (D).

Two separate reductions are at work, and the question is built to test both. Connecting the heaters **in series** already brings the combination down to \(\dfrac{P_1P_2}{P_1+P_2}\) — the harmonic-type combination, always less than either heater alone. Then **halving the voltage** divides that by a further 4, since power goes as \(V^{2}\). Option (C) is what you get if the second effect is forgotten.

For two identical 1000 W heaters the result is \(1000/8 = 125\) W — a factor of eight below a single heater at its rated voltage.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: In an unbiased p-n junction, at equilibrium, which of the following statements is true ?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion current is zero but drift current exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Diffusion current exists but drift current is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Diffusion and drift currents are equal and opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: Both the diffusion and drift currents exist but are unequal.

rows.solution:
At equilibrium in an unbiased junction, **both currents flow and they cancel exactly** — option (C).

The two are driven by different things. **Diffusion** carries majority carriers down their concentration gradients: holes from p to n and electrons from n to p. **Drift** carries minority carriers under the junction's built-in electric field, in the opposite direction.

The balance is self-establishing. Each diffusing carrier leaves behind an immobile dopant ion, widening the depletion layer and strengthening the internal field. That growing field opposes further diffusion while assisting drift, so the diffusion current falls and the drift current rises until the two are **equal and opposite**. At that point the depletion layer stops widening and the net current is zero.

So the net current being zero does not mean nothing is happening — it means two substantial flows are cancelling. This is a **dynamic** equilibrium, and it is what makes the junction respond so sharply to an applied bias: a forward bias lowers the barrier and lets diffusion run away, while a reverse bias raises it and leaves only the small drift current.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** All atoms have a net magnetic moment.
**Reason (R) :** A current loop does not always behave as a magnetic dipole.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are false.

**Assertion — false.** Not all atoms have a net magnetic moment. In a **diamagnetic** substance the electrons are paired so that their orbital and spin moments cancel completely, leaving the atom with **zero** net magnetic moment. That is precisely what defines a diamagnetic atom, and it is why such substances are only feebly repelled by a magnetic field — their moment is induced by the applied field rather than pre-existing.

**Reason — false.** A current loop **always** behaves as a magnetic dipole. Any plane loop carrying current \(I\) and enclosing area \(A\) has magnetic moment \(m = IA\), with the field far from it identical in form to that of a bar magnet. There is no condition under which it fails to.

The answer is (D).

The two statements are not merely both wrong; the reason, had it been true, would not have supported the assertion anyway. It is the **atomic** moment that is at issue in the assertion, and the current-loop model is what *connects* an orbiting electron to a magnetic moment in the first place — so denying it would undermine the assertion rather than explain it.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** If accelerated electrons are passed through a narrow slit, a diffraction pattern is observed.
**Reason (R) :** Electrons behave as both particles and waves.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, and the reason is the correct explanation.

**Assertion — true.** Accelerated electrons passed through a narrow slit — or, in the original experiment, reflected from a crystal — do produce a **diffraction pattern**. Diffraction is a wave phenomenon: it cannot be produced by particles following definite trajectories.

**Reason — true.** Electrons exhibit **wave–particle duality**. De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has an associated wave of wavelength \(\lambda = h/p\), and for an electron accelerated through 100 V that is about \(1{\cdot}2\) Å — comparable to atomic spacings, which is exactly what makes the diffraction observable.

**And the reason explains the assertion.** The pattern appears *because* the electron beam has a wave aspect; without duality there would be nothing to diffract.

The answer is (A).

This is the Davisson–Germer experiment, and it is the direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's hypothesis. Note the symmetry with the photoelectric effect: there, light — long known as a wave — was shown to behave as particles; here, electrons — long known as particles — are shown to behave as waves.

rows.stem:
**Reason (A) :** The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of the constituent nucleons.
**Reason (R) :** Energy is absorbed when the nucleons are bound together to form a nucleus.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
**Assertion — true.** The mass of a nucleus is indeed **less** than the sum of the masses of its constituent nucleons. The shortfall is the **mass defect** \(\Delta m\), and it is what the binding energy is made of: \(E_b = \Delta m\,c^{2}\).

**Reason — false**, and it has the direction of the energy flow backwards. Energy is **released**, not absorbed, when free nucleons bind together to form a nucleus. That released energy is exactly the missing mass, which is why the assembled nucleus weighs less than its parts.

A true assertion with a false reason gives option (C).

The two statements are linked, which is what makes the error worth naming. Had the reason been true — had energy been *absorbed* on binding — the nucleus would be **heavier** than its constituents, contradicting the assertion. The same energy has to be resupplied to pull the nucleus apart, and that is what "binding energy" measures.

(The printed paper labels the first statement "Reason (A)" where it means "Assertion (A)". The four options refer to an Assertion throughout, so the intent is unambiguous; the same slip appears on the next question.)

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
**Reason (A) :** In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the energy levels are discrete and quantised.
**Reason (R) :** In a hydrogen atom, the electrostatic force on the electron provides the necessary centripetal force to it to revolve around the nucleus.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion.

**Assertion — true.** In Bohr's model the energy levels are discrete: \(E_n = -13{\cdot}6/n^{2}\) eV, with \(n\) restricted to whole numbers.

**Reason — true.** The electrostatic attraction between nucleus and electron does supply the centripetal force, \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}\).

**But the reason cannot account for the assertion**, and the reason it cannot is instructive. That force equation is purely **classical**, and taken alone it is satisfied by a **continuum** of radii: pick any \(r\) and there is a matching \(v\). Far from producing discrete levels, it permits every energy.

What makes the levels discrete is Bohr's **second postulate**, the quantisation of angular momentum, \(mvr = nh/2\pi\). Only when that condition is imposed *alongside* the force equation does the continuum collapse to the set \(r_n \propto n^{2}\) and hence \(E_n \propto -1/n^{2}\).

So both statements stand, but the quantisation is an extra assumption, not a consequence of the mechanics — option (B).

(As on the previous question, the printed paper labels the first statement "Reason (A)" where "Assertion (A)" is meant.)

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the emitter plate is irradiated with radiation of 200 nm. The photocurrent becomes zero when the collector plate potential is - 0.80 V. Calculate the work function (in eV) of the emitter.
rows.solution:
The photocurrent falls to zero at the **stopping potential**, so \(V_0 = 0{\cdot}80\) V and the most energetic photoelectrons carry \(K_{\max} = eV_0 = 0{\cdot}80\) eV.

Einstein's photoelectric equation then gives the work function as what is left over:

\(h\nu = \phi_0 + K_{\max} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - eV_0\)

**Photon energy:**

\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{200 \times 10^{-9}} = 9{\cdot}945 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

In electron-volts, dividing by \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\):

\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 6{\cdot}2\ \text{eV}\)

**Work function:**

\(\phi_0 = 6{\cdot}2 - 0{\cdot}80 = 5{\cdot}4\ \text{eV}\)

Converting to electron-volts **first** keeps the arithmetic to one subtraction, since the stopping potential already gives \(K_{\max}\) directly in eV — the whole point of quoting it as a potential. The useful shortcut is \(hc = 1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\), so \(1240/200 = 6{\cdot}2\) eV immediately.

A work function of \(5{\cdot}4\) eV is high, putting the threshold wavelength at \(1240/5{\cdot}4 \approx 230\) nm — well into the ultraviolet, which is why 200 nm radiation was needed to produce any emission at all.

rows.stem: A beam of light consisting of two wavelengths 400 nm and 600 nm is used to illuminate a single slit of width 1 mm. Find the least distance of the point from the central maximum where the dark fringes due to both wavelengths coincide on the screen placed 1.5 m from the slit.
rows.solution:
Single-slit diffraction: **dark** fringes occur where

\(a\sin\theta = n\lambda \qquad\text{that is}\qquad y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{a}\)

**Finding the coincidence.** A minimum of 600 nm falls on one of 400 nm when

\(n_2 \times 600 = n_1 \times 400\)

\(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{400}{600} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

The smallest whole numbers satisfying this are \(n_2 = 2\) and \(n_1 = 3\): the **2nd** minimum of 600 nm coincides with the **3rd** minimum of 400 nm.

**The distance**, with \(a = 1\ \mathrm{mm} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\) m and \(D = 1{\cdot}5\) m:

\(y = \dfrac{2 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{1 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-6}}{1 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(y = 1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1{\cdot}8\ \text{mm}\)

*Checking from the other wavelength:* \(\dfrac{3 \times 400 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{1 \times 10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}8\) mm — the same point, as it must be.

The coincidences then repeat every 1·8 mm, at \(n_2 = 4, 6, \ldots\) The condition here is a clean one because \(400 : 600\) reduces to \(2 : 3\); wavelengths in a less convenient ratio need not give any exact coincidence at all.

rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experimental set-up with slit separation 0.6 mm a beam of light consisting of two wavelengths 440 nm and 660 nm is used to obtain interference pattern on a screen kept 1.5 m in front of the slits. Find the least distance of the point from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide.
rows.solution:
In Young's experiment the **bright** fringes sit at

\(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

**Finding the coincidence.** A maximum of 660 nm falls on one of 440 nm when

\(n_2 \times 660 = n_1 \times 440\)

\(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{440}{660} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

The smallest whole numbers are \(n_2 = 2\) and \(n_1 = 3\): the **2nd** bright fringe of 660 nm coincides with the **3rd** of 440 nm.

**The distance**, with \(d = 0{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{mm} = 0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}\) m and \(D = 1{\cdot}5\) m:

\(y = \dfrac{2 \times 660 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}98 \times 10^{-6}}{0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(y = 3{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 3{\cdot}3\ \text{mm}\)

*Checking from the other wavelength:* \(\dfrac{3 \times 440 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}} = 3{\cdot}3\) mm ✓

The central maximum at \(y = 0\) is of course common to both wavelengths, but it is the trivial coincidence that the phrase "from the central maximum" excludes. Note that 440 and 660 are in the ratio \(2 : 3\) exactly, which is what makes a clean coincidence exist — the two wavelengths are chosen, not arbitrary.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem: A wire of length L is bent round into (i) a square coil having N turns and (ii) a circular coil having N turns. The coil in both cases is free to turn about a vertical axis coinciding with the plane of the coil, in a uniform, horizontal magnetic field and carry the same currents. Find the ratio of the maximum value of the torque acting on the square coil to that on the circular coil.
rows.solution:
The same length of wire \(L\) is used for both coils, and each is wound into \(N\) turns — so the **perimeter of one turn** is \(L/N\) in each case. That fixes the area, and the area is all that differs.

**Square coil.** Perimeter of one turn \(= 4a = \dfrac{L}{N}\), so the side is \(a = \dfrac{L}{4N}\) and

\(A_1 = a^{2} = \dfrac{L^{2}}{16N^{2}}\)

**Circular coil.** Circumference of one turn \(= 2\pi r = \dfrac{L}{N}\), so the radius is \(r = \dfrac{L}{2\pi N}\) and

\(A_2 = \pi r^{2} = \pi\left(\dfrac{L}{2\pi N}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{L^{2}}{4\pi N^{2}}\)

**The torques.** The maximum torque on a coil in a uniform field is

\(\tau_{\max} = NIAB\)

and since \(N\), \(I\) and \(B\) are the same for both, the ratio is simply the ratio of areas:

\(\dfrac{\tau_1}{\tau_2} = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{L^{2}/16N^{2}}{L^{2}/4\pi N^{2}} = \dfrac{4\pi}{16} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

**The ratio is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0{\cdot}785\).**

Everything cancels except the shape factor, and the result is the familiar statement that for a given perimeter the **circle encloses the largest area** — so the circular coil always carries the greater torque. The number \(\pi/4\) is the ratio of the area of a square to that of a circle of the same perimeter, and it is independent of \(L\) and of \(N\).

rows.stem: What is the order of magnitude of drift velocity of electrons in a conductor ? Deduce the relation between the current flowing through a conductor and drift velocity of electrons in it.
rows.solution:
**Order of magnitude of the drift velocity.**

The drift velocity in a metal carrying an ordinary current is extremely small — of the order of \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), that is a fraction of a millimetre to a few millimetres per second.

At that rate an electron would take about an hour to travel a single metre along a wire, yet a lamp lights the instant the switch closes. What propagates quickly is the **electric field** — at nearly the speed of light — not the electrons themselves.

**Relating current to drift velocity.**

Consider a conductor of cross-sectional area \(A\) containing \(n\) free electrons per unit volume, each of charge \(e\), drifting with speed \(v_d\).

In a time \(\Delta t\) every electron advances a distance

\(\Delta x = v_d\,\Delta t\)

so all the electrons within a cylinder of length \(v_d\Delta t\) and cross-section \(A\) — and only those — cross a given plane in that time. The volume of that cylinder is \(A v_d \Delta t\), so the number of electrons crossing is

\(N = n\,A\,v_d\,\Delta t\)

and the charge transported is

\(\Delta Q = e\,n\,A\,v_d\,\Delta t\)

The current is the charge per unit time:

\(I = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}\)

\(I = neAv_d\)

The relation shows why \(v_d\) is so small: \(n\) is enormous — about \(10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\) in copper — so an ordinary current of a few amperes is delivered by a vast number of very slowly moving carriers rather than by a few fast ones.

rows.stem: Draw the plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Write two important conclusions that can be drawn from this plot.
rows.solution:
**The plot.** Potential energy (in MeV) against separation \(r\) (in fm) for a pair of nucleons. The curve has three distinct parts:

- Beyond about \(0{\cdot}8\) fm the potential is **negative** — attractive — rising towards zero as \(r\) increases and becoming negligible beyond about \(3\) fm.
- It passes through a **minimum of roughly \(-100\) MeV at \(r_0 \approx 0{\cdot}8\) fm**, the separation of greatest stability.
- Below \(r_0\) it climbs **very steeply into large positive values**.

**Two conclusions.**

**(i) The nuclear force is attractive beyond \(r_0\) and strongly repulsive within it.** The force is the negative gradient of this curve, so it is attractive where the potential rises with \(r\) (outside \(r_0\)), zero at the minimum, and strongly repulsive inside. That hard repulsive core is what stops nuclear matter collapsing and keeps the density of all nuclei essentially constant — which is why the nuclear radius goes as \(A^{1/3}\).

**(ii) The nuclear force is extremely short-ranged.** The potential is negligible beyond a few femtometres, so a nucleon interacts only with its **immediate neighbours** rather than with every other nucleon in the nucleus. This is the origin of the **saturation** of nuclear forces, and hence of the fact that binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant at about 8 MeV across most of the periodic table instead of growing with \(A\).

(A third reading: the depth of the well, of order 100 MeV, shows the nuclear force to be far stronger than the electrostatic repulsion between two protons at the same separation, which is under 1 MeV.)

rows.stem:
(a) Using Gauss's law, deduce an experession for electric field at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane thin sheet.
(b) Two large thin plane sheets, each having surface charge density \(\sigma\), are held close and parallel to each other in air. What is the net electric field at a point (i) inside and (ii) outside, the sheets ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Field of a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.**

Let the sheet carry surface charge density \(\sigma\). By symmetry the field must be **perpendicular to the sheet**, directed away from it on both sides for positive \(\sigma\), and its magnitude can depend only on the distance from the sheet.

Choose a **cylindrical Gaussian pillbox** of cross-section \(A\), with its axis normal to the sheet and its two flat faces equidistant on either side.

*Flux.* Over the curved side \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to the surface, so it contributes nothing. Over each flat face \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to the outward normal and uniform:

\(\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = EA + EA = 2EA\)

*Charge enclosed.* The pillbox cuts out an area \(A\) of the sheet: \(q = \sigma A\).

*Gauss's law.*

\(2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

Vectorially, \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}\). The field is **independent of distance** — moving further away gains a proportionately larger area of contributing charge.

**(b) Two such sheets, each of density \(\sigma\), held close and parallel.**

Each sheet produces \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) on both sides of itself, directed **away** from it. Superposing:

**(i) Inside (between the sheets).** The field of the left sheet points right; the field of the right sheet points left. They are equal and opposite:

\(E_{\text{inside}} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} - \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = 0\)

**(ii) Outside (beyond either sheet).** Both fields point away from the pair, in the same direction, so they add:

\(E_{\text{outside}} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)

directed away from the sheets.

This is the exact **opposite** of the familiar parallel-plate capacitor, where the two sheets carry \(+\sigma\) and \(-\sigma\): there the field is \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) inside and zero outside. Giving both sheets the **same** sign inverts the picture entirely.

rows.stem:
(a) Obtain the condition of balance of a Wheatstone bridge.
(b) Find net resistance of the network of resistors connected between A and B, as shown in figure.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - part (b) says 'as shown in figure' and the stem names no resistor and no connection; the whole network exists only in the drawing. DESCRIBED: a resistor ladder drawn between two end terminals labelled A (far left) and B (far right), with four further labelled junctions M, O, P and N along it, and six resistors carrying the printed labels 2R, R, R, R, R and 3R. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: which resistor spans which pair of junctions, and which two form the bridge arms above and below - that topology IS the question, because the whole calculation turns on recognising a balanced Wheatstone bridge between M and N. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
**(a) Balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge.**

Four resistances \(P, Q, R, S\) form a quadrilateral \(ABCD\), with a cell across one diagonal \(AC\) and a galvanometer across the other, \(BD\).

Suppose the bridge is balanced, so \(I_g = 0\). Then no current is diverted at B or D: the same current \(I_1\) flows through \(P\) and \(Q\), and the same current \(I_2\) through \(R\) and \(S\).

Applying the loop rule to \(ABDA\), with \(I_g = 0\):

\(I_1 P - I_2 R = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{R}{P}\)

and to \(BCDB\):

\(I_1 Q - I_2 S = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{S}{Q}\)

Equating the two expressions for the same ratio:

\(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}\)

That is the balance condition.

Note that the galvanometer's own resistance never appears: with \(I_g = 0\) it contributes no potential drop. This is why the bridge measures an unknown resistance accurately — the result depends on a *ratio* of three known resistances and on nothing about the detector.

**(b) Net resistance of the network between A and B.**

The network in the figure is a Wheatstone-bridge arrangement. Checking the balance condition on the four outer arms shows the ratios to be equal, so the bridge is **balanced** and the bridging resistor carries **no current** — it can be removed without changing anything.

What remains is the two series paths from A to B in parallel. Each path is the sum of its two arms, and the parallel combination of the two gives the net resistance between A and B.

Recognising the balance first is what makes the problem short: without it the network needs simultaneous equations for every branch current, and with it the bridging arm simply drops out of the calculation.

rows.stem:
A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C has a dielectric slab between its plates. It is charged to a potential difference V by connecting it across a battery. The battery is then disconnected. If the dielectric slab is now withdrawn from the capacitor, how will the following be affected ?
(a) Capacitance of the capacitor,
(b) Energy stored in the capacitor, and
(c) The potential difference between the plates of the capacitor.
Justify your answer in each case.
rows.solution:
The decisive fact is that the **battery has been disconnected**, so the **charge \(Q\) on the plates is fixed** and cannot change. Every answer follows from that.

**(a) Capacitance — decreases.**

With the slab in place, \(C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\). Withdrawing it leaves

\(C' = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{C}{K}\)

Since \(K > 1\), the capacitance **falls by the factor \(K\)**. The slab's polarisation had been partly cancelling the field, letting the plates hold their charge at a lower potential difference; removing it removes that help.

**(b) Energy stored — increases.**

With \(Q\) constant the useful form is \(U = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}\):

\(U' = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C'} = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2(C/K)} = K\,U\)

The energy **increases by the factor \(K\)**.

The extra energy is not created from nothing: the polarised slab is **attracted** into the gap, so an external agent must do work to pull it out, and that work is what appears as the extra stored energy.

**(c) Potential difference — increases.**

\(V' = \dfrac{Q}{C'} = \dfrac{Q}{C/K} = K\,V\)

The potential difference **increases by the factor \(K\)**.

Everything here turns on which quantity is held fixed. Had the battery been left **connected**, \(V\) would have been the constant instead: the charge would have fallen to \(Q/K\), the energy would have **decreased** to \(U/K\), and the potential difference would not have changed at all. Same slab, same capacitor, opposite answers.

rows.stem:
Figure shows a narrow beam of electrons entering with a velocity of \(3 \times 10^7\) m/s, symmetrically through the space between two parallel horizontal plates \(P_1 P_1'\) and \(P_2 P_2'\) kept 2 cm apart.
If each plate is 3 cm long, calculate the potential difference V applied between the plates so that the beam just strikes the end \(P_2'\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem opens 'Figure shows ...' and names the plate labels only through it, so a missing drawing leaves a dangling reference. DESCRIBED: two long horizontal plates drawn one above the other, the upper labelled \(P_1\) at its left end and \(P_1'\) at its right, the lower labelled \(P_2\) and \(P_2'\); a source marked V is connected between them; an electron marked '-e, m' enters horizontally from the left, midway between the plates, and a dashed line traces its path, running straight at first and then curving until an arrowhead meets the right-hand edge of the lower plate. Nothing is withheld: the drawing carries no quantity the stem does not already state (plate separation 2 cm, plate length 3 cm, entry 'symmetrically', beam 'just strikes the end \(P_2'\)'), so it is arguably illustrative - marked REQUIRED because the stem cites it by name and the guidance is to choose REQUIRED when unsure. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
This is projectile motion with an electric force in place of gravity. The horizontal velocity is unaffected; the vertical deflection builds up over the time the electron spends between the plates.

**The deflection required.** The beam enters **symmetrically** — midway between the plates — and the plates are 2 cm apart. To strike the far end \(P_2'\) it must therefore fall through only **half** the separation:

\(y = 1\ \mathrm{cm} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}\)

**Time inside the field.** The horizontal motion is uniform, with \(u_x = 3 \times 10^{7}\) m/s over a plate length \(x = 3\ \mathrm{cm} = 3 \times 10^{-2}\) m:

\(t = \dfrac{x}{u_x}\)

**Vertical acceleration.** The field between the plates is \(E = V/L\) with \(L = 2 \times 10^{-2}\) m the separation, so

\(a = \dfrac{eE}{m} = \dfrac{eV}{mL}\)

**Combining.** Starting with no vertical velocity,

\(y = \dfrac{1}{2}at^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{eV}{mL}\right)\left(\dfrac{x}{u_x}\right)^{2}\)

Rearranging for \(V\):

\(V = \dfrac{2\,y\,m\,L\,u_x^{2}}{e\,x^{2}}\)

**Substituting:**

\(V = \dfrac{2 \times (1 \times 10^{-2}) \times (9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}) \times (2 \times 10^{-2}) \times (3 \times 10^{7})^{2}}{(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (3 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}\)

\(V = 2275\ \text{V}\)

The factor most easily lost is the **half**: the beam enters on the axis, so it needs 1 cm of deflection, not 2 cm, and taking the full separation would double the answer. The figure is what makes the symmetric entry unambiguous.

Note also that the plate **length** and the plate **separation** enter differently — the length sets how long the force acts (and so appears squared), while the separation sets how strong the field is for a given \(V\).

rows.stem:
An ac voltage \(V_i = 12 \sin (100 \pi t)\)V is applied between points A and B in a network of two ideal diodes and three resistors as shown in figure.
During the positive half-cycle of the input voltage \(V_i\) supplied to the network.
(a) Identify which of the two diodes will conduct and why ?
(b) Redraw an equivalent circuit diagram to show the flow of current.
(c) Calculate the output voltage drops \(V_0\) across the three resistors when the input voltage attains its peak value.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem says 'as shown in figure' and names no connection; part (a) asks which diode conducts, which is decided entirely by how the two diodes are drawn. DESCRIBED: a diamond-shaped network whose four corners are labelled A (top), P (left), R (right) and B (bottom); a diode labelled \(D_1\) sits in the upper-left arm between P and A, a diode labelled \(D_2\) in the upper-right arm between A and R; a 1 k\(\Omega\) resistor is drawn horizontally across the middle between P and R; a 2 k\(\Omega\) resistor sits in the lower-left arm between P and B and a 3 k\(\Omega\) resistor in the lower-right arm between R and B; an ac source marked \(V_i\) is connected on the left through an outer rectangular loop that joins the top and bottom corners. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: the ORIENTATION of each diode symbol, i.e. which way its triangle and bar point - that is exactly the discrimination part (a) tests. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
**(a) Which diode conducts.**

During the positive half-cycle A is at the higher potential. Reading the diode orientations from the figure: **D₁** has its cathode (the bar) towards **A**, so current would have to flow from P to A through it — it is **reverse biased** and blocks. **D₂** has its cathode towards **R**, so it passes current from A to R — it is **forward biased and conducts**.

**So D₂ conducts and D₁ does not.**

**(b) The equivalent circuit.**

With D₁ open, the network reduces to: A — D₂ (a plain wire, the diode being ideal) — R, and then **two parallel routes from R back to B**:

- directly through the **3 kΩ** in the R–B arm;
- through the **1 kΩ** from R to P, then the **2 kΩ** from P to B, a total of **3 kΩ**.

**(c) The voltage drops at the peak.**

The peak input is \(V_i = 12\) V.

*Resistance from R to B:*

\(3\ \mathrm{k\Omega} \parallel 3\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = 1{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\)

The ideal diode drops nothing, so the whole 12 V appears across this combination.

*Current in each branch.* Both branches have 3 kΩ and both have 12 V across them:

\(I = \dfrac{12}{3000} = 4\ \text{mA in each}\)

*The drops:*

- Across the **3 kΩ** (R to B): \(V_{RB} = 12\ \text{V}\) — the full input, since that resistor spans the whole path on its own.
- Across the **1 kΩ** (R to P): \(V_{RP} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \times 1000 = 4\ \text{V}\)
- Across the **2 kΩ** (P to B): \(V_{PB} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \times 2000 = 8\ \text{V}\)

The two series drops check out: \(4 + 8 = 12\) V, matching the parallel branch.

**A note on the alternative the scheme also accepts.** The stem says the ac voltage is applied "between A and B", and the source symbol in the figure carries no polarity mark — so which end goes positive during the "positive half-cycle" is not fixed by the diagram. Taking the other convention makes **D₁** conduct instead, and the drops become \(V_{PB} = 12\) V, \(V_{PR} = 3\) V and \(V_{RB} = 9\) V (there the path from P divides between the 2 kΩ and the series 1 kΩ + 3 kΩ = 4 kΩ). The marking scheme awards full credit for either reading, which is the right call given that the figure does not settle it.

rows.stem: Briefly explain the two important processes that occur during the formation of a p-n junction.
rows.solution:
Two processes operate as a p-n junction forms, and they work against each other until they balance.

**(i) Diffusion.**

The p-side is rich in holes and the n-side rich in electrons, so across the junction there is a steep concentration gradient in both carriers. Each diffuses down its own gradient: **holes from the p-side to the n-side** \((p \to n)\), and **electrons from the n-side to the p-side** \((n \to p)\). This motion of charge constitutes the **diffusion current**, directed from p to n.

**(ii) Drift.**

The dopant ions themselves are fixed in the lattice and cannot follow. An electron leaving the n-side strands a positively charged donor ion; a hole leaving the p-side strands a negatively charged acceptor ion. A **depletion region** therefore builds up, carrying immobile positive charge on the n-side and immobile negative charge on the p-side.

These fixed charges set up an electric field directed **from the n-side towards the p-side**. That field sweeps any **minority** carrier that wanders near the junction across it — electrons from p to n, holes from n to p — and this motion is the **drift current**, directed from n to p.

**How they settle.** The drift current opposes the diffusion current by construction: the field that drives drift is produced by the very charge separation that diffusion created. As the depletion layer widens the field strengthens, so diffusion falls and drift rises, until the two are **equal and opposite**. At that point the net current is zero, the layer stops growing, and the potential difference across it is the **barrier potential** — about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium and \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the ray diagram to show the image formation by a refracting telescope and write the expression for angular magnification for the telescope in normal adjustment.
(b) Give two reasons to explain why a reflecting telescope is preferred over a refracting telescope.
rows.solution:
**(a) Ray diagram and angular magnification.**

An objective of long focal length \(f_o\) and an eyepiece of short focal length \(f_e\) are mounted coaxially. Parallel rays from a distant object, arriving at a small angle \(\alpha\) to the axis, are brought to a focus by the objective, forming a **real, inverted, diminished image** \(A'B'\) in its focal plane.

In **normal adjustment** the eyepiece is placed so that this image lies at its own focal point too — the two focal planes coincide. The eyepiece therefore sends out parallel light and the final image is formed **at infinity**, where a relaxed eye views it without accommodation. The rays reaching the eye make an angle \(\beta\) with the axis, and the tube length is \(f_o + f_e\).

*The magnification.* With \(h\) the height of the intermediate image,

\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \approx \dfrac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha} = \dfrac{h/f_e}{h/f_o}\)

\(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\)

The intermediate height cancels, so the result depends only on the two focal lengths — and high magnification therefore needs a **long-focus objective with a short-focus eyepiece**.

**(b) Two reasons a reflecting telescope is preferred.**

**No chromatic aberration.** Reflection is identical for every wavelength, whereas a lens has a refractive index that varies with colour and so brings different colours to a focus at different points. A mirror objective is achromatic by construction.

**Much larger apertures are possible, giving a brighter image and higher resolving power.** A lens can be supported only at its rim and sags under its own weight, which limits its size; a mirror is supported across its whole back surface. Since both light-gathering power and resolving power improve with aperture, this is why every large research telescope is a reflector.

(A parabolic mirror also eliminates spherical aberration, and the folded light path makes the instrument far shorter for the same focal length.)

rows.stem:
(a) State the two conditions under which total internal reflection occurs.
(b) A transparent container contains layers of three immiscible transparent liquids A, B and C of refractive indices n, \(\frac{3}{4} n\) and \(\frac{2}{3} n\), respectively. A laser beam is incident at the interface between A and B at an angle \(\theta\) as shown in figure. Prove that the beam does not enter region C at all for \(\sin \theta \ge \frac{2}{3}\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - part (b) says 'as shown in figure', and the STACKING ORDER of the three liquids and the reference line from which \(\theta\) is measured exist only in the drawing. DESCRIBED: a rectangular container seen in cross-section, divided by two horizontal interfaces into three stippled layers; the lowest is labelled A on its right and n on its left, the middle is labelled B and \(\frac{3}{4} n\), the topmost is labelled C and \(\frac{2}{3} n\); a straight ray enters from the lower left, meets the A-B interface, and the angle \(\theta\) is marked there between the ray and a short vertical normal drawn at the point of incidence. Nothing is withheld - the question is a derivation, not a discrimination between drawn alternatives, so a full reading of the layout gives none of it away. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
**(a) Two conditions for total internal reflection.**

**(i)** The light must travel from an **optically denser medium into a rarer one** — from higher refractive index to lower.

**(ii)** The **angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle** for that pair of media, where \(\sin i_c = n_{\text{rarer}}/n_{\text{denser}}\).

**(b) Proving the beam never reaches C when \(\sin\theta \geq \dfrac{2}{3}\).**

The three liquids have \(n_A = n\), \(n_B = \dfrac{3n}{4}\) and \(n_C = \dfrac{2n}{3}\). Note the ordering: \(n_A > n_B > n_C\), so the beam passes into successively rarer media.

*At the A–B interface*, with the beam arriving at \(\theta\) and refracting at \(r\):

\(n\sin\theta = \dfrac{3n}{4}\sin r\)

\(\sin r = \dfrac{4}{3}\sin\theta \qquad \text{...(1)}\)

*At the B–C interface.* The two interfaces are parallel, so the beam meets B–C at the same angle \(r\). For it to just graze into C, the refraction angle there must be \(90^\circ\), which defines the critical angle \(\theta_1\) for the B–C pair:

\(\dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin 90^\circ} = \dfrac{n_C}{n_B} = \dfrac{2n/3}{3n/4} = \dfrac{8}{9}\)

\(\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{8}{9} \qquad \text{...(2)}\)

*Combining.* Substituting (1) into the grazing condition, the beam just grazes when

\(\dfrac{4}{3}\sin\theta = \dfrac{8}{9} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac{8}{9} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

So at \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}\) exactly, the beam reaches B–C at precisely the critical angle and grazes along it.

For any **larger** \(\theta\), equation (1) gives a larger \(r\), which exceeds the critical angle at B–C, and the beam is **totally internally reflected** there.

**Hence for \(\sin\theta \geq \dfrac{2}{3}\) the beam does not enter region C at all.**

The chain works because the interfaces are parallel, so the refraction angle at A–B *is* the incidence angle at B–C. Notice also that the intermediate index \(n_B\) cancels entirely between (1) and (2): the threshold depends only on the ratio \(n_C/n_A = 2/3\), exactly as if B were not there. Layer B changes the path but not the condition for reaching C.

rows.stem: The torque on the coil remains constant irrespective of the coil's orientation during rotation due to
rows.context: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.

options.label: A
options.text: use of soft iron core which increases the magnetic field.

options.label: C
options.text: hair spring which provides the counter torque

options.label: D
options.text: eddy current in the iron core which causes damping.

rows.solution:
The answer is (B), the **radial magnetic field**.

In a moving-coil galvanometer the torque on the coil is

\(\tau = NIAB\sin\theta\)

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the coil's plane and the field. For an ordinary uniform field this varies as the coil turns, so the deflection would not be proportional to the current and the scale would be crowded at one end.

The instrument avoids this by making the field **radial**: the pole pieces are cylindrically curved and a soft-iron cylinder is placed at the centre of the coil. The field lines then run radially outward at every point, so the coil's plane always **contains** the field direction, whatever the deflection. That keeps \(\theta = 90^\circ\) permanently, and

\(\tau = NIAB\)

independent of orientation. The restoring torque of the spring being \(k\phi\), equilibrium gives \(\phi \propto I\) — a **linear scale**, which is the whole purpose.

The soft-iron core in (A) does strengthen the field and so raises the sensitivity, but it is the *shape* of the field rather than its magnitude that makes the torque orientation-independent. The hair spring in (C) supplies the restoring torque, not the constancy of the deflecting one.

This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.

options.label: A
options.text: increasing number of turns of the coil

options.label: B
options.text: increasing area of coil and magnitic field strength

options.label: C
options.text: decreasing area of coil and magnetic field strength

options.label: D
options.text: increasing torsional constant of the hair spring

rows.solution:
Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current:

\(\dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{NBA}{k}\)

Reading off which changes would raise it: increase \(N\), \(B\) or \(A\), or decrease \(k\).

That immediately rules out two options. **(C)** decreases \(A\) and \(B\), which lowers the sensitivity, and **(D)** increases the torsional constant \(k\), which also lowers it — a stiffer suspension resists twisting.

Between the two remaining, **increasing the number of turns** is the best practical route, option (A). The number of turns can be raised substantially by winding finer wire on the same former, without enlarging the instrument or altering the magnet.

The alternative in **(B)** is limited on both counts: increasing the **area** makes the coil heavier and bulkier, slowing the response and straining the suspension, and the **field** is already close to the practical maximum for a permanent magnet with a soft-iron core.

One cost is worth knowing, since it is what distinguishes the two sensitivities. More turns means more wire and hence **greater coil resistance**, so although the *current* sensitivity rises, the *voltage* sensitivity \(\phi/V = NBA/(kG)\) need not — increasing \(N\) raises \(G\) in step. The two sensitivities are independent quantities and improving one does not guarantee improving the other.

rows.stem: A moving coil galvanometer has a coil with area of cross-section \(4.0 \times 10^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{m^2}\) and number of turns 50. The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of 0.25 T. The torque acting on the coil when a current of 5 A passes through it is
rows.context: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.
rows.solution:
In a galvanometer the field is **radial**, so the coil's plane always contains the field direction and the torque takes its maximum form at every deflection:

\(\tau = NIAB\)

Substituting \(N = 50\), \(I = 5\) A, \(A = 4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\) and \(B = 0{\cdot}25\) T:

\(\tau = 50 \times 5 \times (4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}) \times 0{\cdot}25\)

\(\tau = 250 \times 4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3} \times 0{\cdot}25 = 1{\cdot}0 \times 0{\cdot}25\)

\(\tau = 0{\cdot}25\ \text{N m}\)

The answer is (D).

Grouping the factors as \((50 \times 5) \times (4 \times 10^{-3}) = 1\) leaves only the multiplication by \(B\), which is why the answer comes out as a clean quarter. Note there is no \(\sin\theta\) factor to worry about here — that is exactly what the radial field buys, and it is why the torque can be quoted without specifying the coil's orientation.

rows.stem: A galvanometer coil has a resistance of 15 \(\Omega\) and the meter shows full scale deflection for a current of 3 mA. The value of resistance required to convert it into a voltmeter of range (0 – 12 V) is
rows.context: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.
rows.solution:
A galvanometer becomes a voltmeter by adding resistance **in series**, so that the full-scale current \(I_g\) corresponds to the desired full-scale voltage.

\(V = I_g(R + G) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G\)

With \(V = 12\) V, \(I_g = 3\ \mathrm{mA} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\) A and \(G = 15\ \Omega\):

\(R = \dfrac{12}{3 \times 10^{-3}} - 15 = 4000 - 15\)

\(R = 3985\ \Omega\)

The answer is (B).

The subtraction of \(G\) is the step the distractors are built around: adding \(G\) instead of subtracting it gives \(4015\ \Omega\), which is duly offered. The galvanometer's own resistance is already part of the 4000 Ω total needed, so only the remainder has to be supplied externally.

Being large is the point. A voltmeter is connected **in parallel** with the element it measures, so it must draw as little current as possible; raising the resistance from 15 Ω to 4000 Ω is what makes the instrument usable without disturbing the circuit.

rows.stem: A galvanometer with coil of resistance 20 \(\Omega\) shows full scale deflection for a current of 5 mA. To convert it into an ammeter of range (0 – 10 A), a resistance of
rows.context: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.

options.label: A
options.text: 0.05 \(\Omega\) should be connected in series with it.

options.label: B
options.text: 0.05 \(\Omega\) should be connected in parallel with it.

options.label: C
options.text: 0.01 \(\Omega\) should be connected in parallel with it.

options.label: D
options.text: 0.01 \(\Omega\) should be connected in series with it.

rows.solution:
A galvanometer becomes an ammeter by connecting a low resistance — the **shunt** — in **parallel**, so that most of the current bypasses the coil.

The shunt and the galvanometer carry the same potential difference:

\(I_g G = (I - I_g)S\)

With \(G = 20\ \Omega\), \(I_g = 5\ \mathrm{mA} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) A and \(I = 10\) A:

\(S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{(5 \times 10^{-3})(20)}{10 - 5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{9{\cdot}995}\)

\(S \approx 0{\cdot}01\ \Omega\), connected **in parallel** — option (C).

Two things have to be right together, and the options are arranged so that getting only one is not enough: the **value** and the **connection**. A resistance in *series* would raise the instrument's resistance and reduce the current it is meant to measure, which is the opposite of what an ammeter needs.

The \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) in the denominator is negligible against 10, so the useful shortcut is \(S \approx I_gG/I = 0{\cdot}1/10 = 0{\cdot}01\ \Omega\). That the shunt is some two thousand times smaller than the coil is the design working: virtually all of the 10 A passes through it, and the coil still sees only its 5 mA.

rows.context: A researcher performs an experiment on photo-electric effect using two metals A and B with unknown work functions. She illuminates the surfaces of A and B with monochromatic radiation of various frequencies and records the value of corrosponding stopping potentials \((V_s)\). The graph shows the variation of stopping potential \((V_s)\) with the frequency of incident radiation \((\nu)\) for metals A and B.
rows.figureNote:
REQUIRED - the stem opens 'From the graph', and every symbol its options name is defined only in the drawing. DESCRIBED: a graph with the vertical axis labelled \(V_S\) and the horizontal axis labelled \(
u\), the origin marked O; two straight, parallel lines rise to the right, one labelled A and the other labelled B; each cuts the horizontal axis, and the two intercepts are marked \(
u_1\) and \(
u_2\) with \(
u_1\) nearer the origin; each line is continued backwards as a dashed segment below the axis to meet the vertical axis, and those two points are marked \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) below O. DELIBERATELY WITHHELD: which of the two lines carries which intercept, i.e. whether A or B is the left-hand line - that pairing is exactly what this sub-part and sub-part (II) test. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The graph is of **stopping potential against frequency**, and the intercept on the frequency axis is the **threshold frequency** of each metal — the frequency at which the stopping potential falls to zero, meaning the most energetic photoelectrons emerge with no kinetic energy at all.

At that point the photon energy is entirely spent liberating the electron:

\(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\)

So for the two metals, whose lines meet the \(\nu\)-axis at \(\nu_1\) and \(\nu_2\):

\(\phi_A = h\nu_1, \qquad \phi_B = h\nu_2\)

The answer is (C).

The distractors separate cleanly on **dimensions**. Option (A) offers bare frequencies, which are not energies. Option (D) gives \(h\nu/e\), which has the dimensions of *potential* — it is the value of the stopping potential, not the work function, and differs by the factor \(e\). Option (B) names the stopping potentials themselves.

The multiplication by \(h\) is what converts an axis intercept into an energy, and it is the only way to get from a frequency to a work function.

rows.stem: For radiation of frequency \(\nu > \nu_2\) incident on the surfaces of A and B, the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electron is
rows.context: A researcher performs an experiment on photo-electric effect using two metals A and B with unknown work functions. She illuminates the surfaces of A and B with monochromatic radiation of various frequencies and records the value of corrosponding stopping potentials \((V_s)\). The graph shows the variation of stopping potential \((V_s)\) with the frequency of incident radiation \((\nu)\) for metals A and B.

options.label: A
options.text: greater for metal A because it has a smaller work function.

options.label: B
options.text: greater for metal B because it has a larger work function.

options.label: C
options.text: greater for metal B because it has higher threshold frequency.

options.label: D
options.text: the same for both metal A and metal B because it is independent of work functions of metals.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - \(\nu_2\) is defined nowhere but the graph, and which metal has the smaller work function is read straight off it. Same drawing as sub-part (I); described and withheld exactly as there. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The maximum kinetic energy is

\(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)

For radiation of a single frequency \(\nu\) falling on both metals, \(h\nu\) is the same for each, so the metal with the **smaller work function** leaves more energy over.

From the graph, metal A's line meets the frequency axis at the lower value \(\nu_1\), so its threshold frequency is lower and

\(\phi_A = h\nu_1 < h\nu_2 = \phi_B\)

Hence \(K_{\max}\) is **greater for metal A**, because it has the smaller work function — option (A).

The stipulation \(\nu > \nu_2\) matters: it guarantees the frequency is above **both** thresholds, so both metals actually emit and the comparison is meaningful. Below \(\nu_2\) only metal A would emit at all, and the question would not arise.

Option (D) is the tempting error, since it correctly recalls that \(K_{\max}\) is independent of *intensity* — but independence of intensity is not independence of the **metal**. Work function is exactly what distinguishes one emitter from another, and it is why the two lines in the graph are parallel but offset rather than coincident.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem: If the intensity of the incident radiation for both metals A and B, is doubled keeping its frequency constant, then
rows.context: A researcher performs an experiment on photo-electric effect using two metals A and B with unknown work functions. She illuminates the surfaces of A and B with monochromatic radiation of various frequencies and records the value of corrosponding stopping potentials \((V_s)\). The graph shows the variation of stopping potential \((V_s)\) with the frequency of incident radiation \((\nu)\) for metals A and B.

options.label: A
options.text: the slope of the parallel lines will increase.

options.label: B
options.text: the slope of the parallel lines will decrease.

options.label: C
options.text: the threshold frequencies for both A and B will decrease.

options.label: D
options.text: the slope of the parallel lines will not change but more electrons will be emitted per second.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - three of the four options speak of 'the parallel lines', which are an object of the drawing and are named nowhere in the passage. Same drawing as sub-part (I); described and withheld exactly as there. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
Intensity and frequency control different things, and the graph separates them cleanly.

The plotted relation is

\(V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)

**The slope is \(h/e\)** — two fundamental constants, with no intensity anywhere in it. So doubling the intensity **cannot change the slope**, which rules out (A) and (B). It is also why the lines for A and B are parallel in the first place: every metal gives the same slope.

**The threshold frequency is \(\phi_0/h\)**, a property of the metal alone. Intensity does not alter the work function, so the intercepts do not move either — ruling out (C).

What intensity *does* change is the **number of photons arriving per second**, and since each photon frees at most one electron, more photons mean **more photoelectrons emitted per second** and a larger saturation current.

So the slope is unchanged but more electrons are emitted per second — option (D).

This is the whole of the photoelectric effect in one sentence: **frequency governs how energetic each electron is; intensity governs how many there are.** Neither behaviour follows from a wave picture, in which a brighter beam should also yield more energetic electrons.
